confidence_note: Book not read; facts come from the publisher's reader's guide, catalogue summaries and Goleman's later reprint. The old 12-20 / 88-80 percent figures were unsourced and dropped. 'Twice as important' is Goleman's claim, disputed by critics.
facts: Working with Emotional Intelligence (1998) follows Goleman's Emotional Intelligence and argues that emotional intelligence matters more than IQ at work and, unlike IQ, can be developed.
Its model groups 25 emotional competencies into five dimensions: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills.
Goleman claims that for star performance in every field, emotional intelligence matters twice as much as IQ or technical expertise; critics say meta-analytic data does not support that claim.
Star performers excel individually and are best at maximizing a team's potential.
Data tracked over decades: team building and adapting to change mattered little in the 1970s but were crucial by the 1990s; change catalyst and leveraging diversity are new star-performer traits.
McClelland found a tipping point at strengths in six or more competencies; stars typically had at least one strength from each cluster.
tension: A claim that emotional skills count twice as much as IQ, and the critics who say the data does not show it.
opening_idea: The 25 competencies sorted into five groups, and the decades of data on what star performers have that others lack.

lessons.idea: Name the five dimensions and rate yourself on each separately, instead of calling yourself 'good with people'.

reflect_final: Which of the five dimensions would a colleague say you lean on least, and what one situation this week would test it?

use_cases.situation: In a team review you want to give feedback on collaboration
use_cases.move: Use the five dimensions as words: ask which one the team leans on least.
Ask which of self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy or social skills they want to build, and pick one situation.
Pick the dimension you rate lowest and one meeting this week to try it in.

pocket_idea: Five groups of emotional skills, not one: name which you lean on least, and test it once this week.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Goleman splits people skills into 25 named competencies in five groups.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Goleman's 1998 model: 25 competencies, five dimensions, a disputed 'twice as important as IQ' claim, and a team-focused picture of star performers.
